title: CMS Hunts a New Particle Using Muons Hiding Inside Protons
hook: A proton is not just quarks and gluons — quantum fluctuations briefly conjure muons inside it. CMS used those fleeting muons to search for a particle that blurs quarks and leptons.
key_points: Leptoquarks are hypothetical particles that couple quarks and leptons directly, which the Standard Model has no room for.
Quantum fluctuations inside a proton generate charged-lepton components, so a muon from one proton can collide with a quark from the other.
That makes a single leptoquark producible on resonance - a first for LHC searches, which usually make them in pairs.
The signature is one or two muons plus a jet; the muon-jet invariant mass would peak at the leptoquark's mass.
CMS found no excess in 138 fb^-1 of 13 TeV data, excluding masses from 1.5 to 3.6 TeV over a broad range of couplings.
content_html: The Standard Model sorts matter into two tidy families — quarks, which feel the strong force and build protons, and leptons like the electron and muon, which do not. Nothing in the theory connects them directly. A leptoquark would: a single particle carrying both quark and lepton charge, coupling the two families together. It shows up in many grand unified theories, and no experiment has ever seen one.
extra_html:
The usual way to look is pair production: make two leptoquarks from a quark-gluon collision, which is straightforward but expensive in energy. The CMS collaboration tried something different in this analysis of 138 fb⁻¹ of 13 TeV proton-proton data. A proton is not a static bag of three quarks; it is a churning cloud of virtual particles, and quantum fluctuations transiently produce charged leptons inside it. That means a muon from one incoming proton can strike a quark from the other — and produce a single leptoquark on resonance, which is far cheaper energetically and reaches higher masses.

The final state is one or two muons plus a jet, from either a light quark or a b quark, and the tell would be a peak in the muon-jet invariant mass. The data matched background predictions, so CMS set upper limits instead. Those limits improve on previous CMS searches, extending coverage to leptoquark masses between 1.5 and 3.6 TeV at couplings from 0.2 to 0.6 in the up-quark scenario, and above 1.8 TeV for b-quark couplings above 1. No discovery — but a genuinely new production channel to keep exploiting.

flashcards.prompt: What is a leptoquark, and why would finding one matter?
flashcards.back_html: A hypothetical particle that couples directly to both a quark and a lepton. The Standard Model keeps quarks and leptons in separate families with no such link, so a leptoquark would be unambiguous physics beyond it.

choices.text: Quantum fluctuations inside a proton briefly generate charged-lepton components, so one proton can supply a muon
The LHC injects muon beams alongside the protons
Protons decay into muons just before collision

flashcards.explanation_html: A proton is a seething mix of virtual particles, including transient charged leptons. A muon from one proton can meet a quark from the other — enabling resonant production of a single leptoquark rather than a pair.

flashcards.prompt: What observable would reveal a leptoquark in this search?
flashcards.back_html: The invariant mass of the muon-jet system. A real leptoquark decaying to a muon and a quark would produce a peak in that distribution at its own mass. CMS saw none.
